title: Several Circles
spot: Find a circle with a tiny black dot in the middle, like an eye. How many can you count?
story: Kandinsky thought colours worked like music — he even named many paintings "Compositions." Does this one look loud or quiet to you?

title: Discomedusae (Art Forms in Nature, plate 8)
spot: This jellyfish is drawn from below and from the side. Follow one long frilly arm from top to bottom.
story: Haeckel was a scientist who drew the sea creatures he studied, many under a microscope. He named thousands of new species.

title: Composition 8
spot: Find the big black circle, a checkerboard and something that looks like a ladder.
story: Kandinsky painted this while teaching at the Bauhaus, a famous German art and design school. It's one of his calmest, most geometric paintings.

title: Banana Flower and Fruit
place: Metamorphosis of the Insects of Surinam
spot: Find the caterpillar and the moth. Could they be the same animal at different ages?
story: In 1699, at age 52, Merian sailed to South America to study insects and how they change — something almost no woman did back then.

title: Castle and Sun
spot: Count the triangles. Can you find the sun?
story: Klee built this whole castle from simple shapes, like building blocks. He was also a very good violin player.

title: Plum Park in Kameido
place: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
spot: Which branch is closest to you? Find the people behind the fence.
story: Hiroshige zoomed in on one branch like a photographer. Van Gogh loved this print so much he painted his own copy.

title: Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow
spot: Which colour has the biggest box? How many rectangles can you count?
story: Mondrian used only straight lines, black, white, grey and three main colours. He wanted the simplest possible picture to feel perfectly balanced.

title: Forest, British Columbia
spot: Find the path that leads deep into the forest. Where do you think it goes?
story: Carr painted the giant trees of the BC coast so they seem to sway and breathe. She was also a writer and won a Governor General's Award.

title: Suprematist Composition: Airplane Flying
spot: Do these shapes look like an airplane to you? Which way is it flying?
story: Malevich wanted paintings with no objects at all — just pure shapes and colour. He called it Suprematism.

title: Trochilidae (Art Forms in Nature)
spot: How many hummingbirds can you count? Which one has the longest tail?
story: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. Their hearts can beat more than 1,000 times a minute.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood
spot: Find spirals, flowers and letters hiding in the swirls.
story: Af Klint painted abstract art years before most famous abstract painters — and asked that it not be shown until 20 years after her death.

title: Silver Sun
spot: Is that a sun, an eye, or something else? What do you see?
story: Dove is often called America's first abstract painter. He tried to paint how nature feels, not just how it looks.

title: Simultaneous Contrasts: Sun and Moon
spot: Where is the sun, and where is the moon?
story: Delaunay was fascinated by how colours seem to change when they sit right next to each other. Try covering half the painting with your hand.

title: North Shore, Lake Superior
spot: What does the tree stump remind you of? Follow the light from the sky.
story: Harris, from Brantford, Ontario, was a founder of the Group of Seven. Later in life his paintings became completely abstract.

title: Senecio
spot: Which eyebrow is raised? What is this face feeling?
story: Klee described drawing as taking a line for a walk. This whole face is built from a circle, squares and triangles.

title: Ascending Forms
spot: Find the black circles stacked like a tower. What's at the very top?
story: In 1927 Brooker showed abstract paintings at the Arts and Letters Club in Toronto — the first abstract art exhibition by a Canadian artist.

title: Yellow-Red-Blue
spot: Find a yellow shape, a red one and a blue one. Which one feels the loudest?
story: Kandinsky believed yellow felt warm and bright, and blue felt calm and deep. Do you agree?

title: Brooklyn Bridge
spot: Find the bridge cables, the arches and the city lights.
story: Stella came to New York from Italy and saw the Brooklyn Bridge as a great cathedral made of steel.

title: Squares with Concentric Circles
spot: Find two squares that use the same colours. Which circle is the smallest?
story: Kandinsky made this as a colour study, testing which colours sing together. It turned into one of his best-loved pictures.

title: On White II
spot: Find the checkerboards, the dice and the black lines shooting across.
story: Kandinsky painted this while teaching at the Bauhaus. He said a white background is like a great silence, full of possibilities.

title: Fish Magic
spot: Find the clock, a flower and as many fish as you can.
story: Klee glued a square of thin cloth onto the middle of this painting. Can you spot its edges?

title: Red Balloon
spot: Find the red balloon. What is it floating over?
story: Klee and Kandinsky both taught at the Bauhaus. For years they lived next door to each other.

title: The Yellow Cow
spot: Is the cow jumping, dancing or running? Find the blue mountains.
story: Marc gave colours feelings. To him yellow meant gentle and cheerful, which is why this cow is anything but brown.

title: Lady in a Green Jacket
spot: Count the people. Who is wearing green? Find the lake behind them.
story: Macke loved bright colours and people strolling in parks. He was killed early in World War I, at just 27.

title: Windows Open Simultaneously
spot: Can you find the green Eiffel Tower hiding among the coloured panes?
story: Delaunay painted light pouring through a window as if it were broken into coloured pieces, like looking through a prism.

title: Painterly Architectonic
spot: Which shape is on top? Which one is at the very back?
story: Popova was a leader of the Russian avant-garde. Later she designed fabrics and stage sets using the same bold shapes.

title: Green Stripe
spot: Are the stripe's edges sharp or soft? Does it look like it's glowing?
story: Rozanova painted a single stripe decades before famous American painters did the same. She died the next year, at just 32.

title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
spot: Find the red wedge and the white circle. Which one seems to be winning?
story: A poster from the Russian Civil War: the red wedge stood for the "Reds" and the white circle for the "Whites." Lissitzky told a story with only shapes.

title: The Cow
spot: Can you find the cow? Hint: it has turned into rectangles.
story: Van Doesburg drew a cow again and again, simplifying each time until only coloured blocks were left. With Mondrian he started the De Stijl movement.

title: I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold
spot: How many 5s can you find? Look for the names BILL and CARLO too.
story: It's a picture of a poem: Demuth's friend William Carlos Williams wrote about a red fire truck numbered 5 racing through the rainy city.

title: Portrait of a German Officer
spot: Find the letters K v F and the number 24.
story: There's no face, but it's a portrait. Hartley made it for his friend Karl von Freyburg, killed in World War I at age 24.

title: Portrait of Félix Fénéon
spot: What is Fénéon holding out? Find the stars behind him.
story: Signac painted it all with tiny dots of pure colour. Fénéon was an art critic who gave this dotty style its name: Neo-Impressionism.

title: The Cyclops
spot: Find the giant's one eye, then the person sleeping on the hillside.
story: In a Greek myth, the cyclops Polyphemus falls in love with the sea nymph Galatea. Redon makes him shy, just peeking over the hill.

title: The Swan, No. 17
spot: Which half is light and which is dark? Find black, white, yellow and blue.
story: Af Klint's Swan series starts with a black swan and a white swan. Painting by painting, they turn into pure shapes about opposites.

title: Snow at Zōjō-ji
spot: Find the person with the umbrella. Is the snow still falling?
story: Hasui made more than 600 prints of Japanese landscapes. Japan later named him a Living National Treasure.

title: Crow and Blossom
spot: Find the crow's eye. How many blossoms are open?
story: Koson made hundreds of bird-and-flower prints, many of them sold to collectors in Europe and America.

title: Kirifuri Waterfall
place: A Tour of the Waterfalls of the Provinces
spot: Find the tiny travellers looking up at the falls.
story: This is by the artist of the famous Great Wave. He drew the water like fingers or roots reaching down the mountain.

title: Actiniae (sea anemones)
spot: These look like flowers, but they're animals! Find one with tentacles like spaghetti.
story: Sea anemones catch food with stinging tentacles. Clownfish are protected from the stings, so they live safely inside them.

title: Totem and Forest
spot: Find the carved faces on the pole. How tall do you think it is?
story: Carr spent years visiting First Nations villages along the BC coast, painting their carved poles among the giant trees.

title: The West Wind
spot: Which way is the wind blowing? How can you tell?
story: Thomson painted the lakes of Algonquin Park, a few hours north of Toronto. You can see this one in person at the AGO.

title: Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2
spot: Find the figure walking down the stairs. How many times can you see it?
story: It shows movement like a stack of photos taken in a row. At a 1913 show in New York, one critic called it "an explosion in a shingle factory."

title: Blue Mountain
spot: Find the riders on horseback at the bottom. Which way are they galloping?
story: Kandinsky painted this in the Bavarian countryside, where his colours broke free of real life: a blue mountain, red and yellow trees.

title: Improvisation 28 (second version)
spot: Look for shapes that almost look like things: a boat, a rainbow, a mountain. What do you find?
story: Kandinsky called his quicker, freer paintings "Improvisations," like a musician making up a tune on the spot.

title: Circles in a Circle
spot: Count the circles inside the big black ring. Where do the coloured beams cross?
story: Kandinsky said the circle was the calmest shape, one that holds all the others in balance.

title: Yellow Accompaniment
spot: Find a checkerboard, a ladder and a black circle.
story: The title is a music word: an accompaniment is the music that plays along with the melody.

title: Highways and Byways
spot: Follow the main road up the middle. How many side roads branch off it?
story: Klee painted this after a trip to Egypt, where he saw fields in neat strips along the river Nile.

title: Portrait of Pablo Picasso
spot: Find Picasso's eyes, his buttons and the palette in his hand.
story: Gris painted his friend Picasso in the new Cubist style they were both exploring, as if seen from many angles at once.

title: Non-Objective Composition
spot: Which shapes look like they are moving fastest?
story: Ekster ran an art studio in Kyiv where young artists learned to paint without pictures. She later designed costumes for theatre and film.

title: Insula Dulcamara
spot: Find a face, a boat and some snake-like lines.
story: One of Klee's biggest paintings, made near the end of his life. The thick black lines look like single strokes of a big brush.

title: Eight Red Rectangles
spot: Count the red rectangles. Are they flying or falling?
story: Some people see fields from an airplane window. Malevich wanted you to feel like you were floating in space.

title: Supremus No. 58
spot: Find the black cross and the yellow lines.
story: Malevich called his style Suprematism because he believed pure shape and colour were "supreme," better than pictures of things.

title: Non-Objective Composition
spot: Find the curve, the red bar and the thin lines like wires.
story: Rodchenko later became famous for photography and posters, shooting buildings from dizzying angles.

title: Electric Prisms
spot: Find the circles that look like glowing street lamps.
story: Sonia Delaunay painted the new electric lights of Paris. She also designed clothes, fabrics and even cars in the same bright patterns.

title: Udnie (The Dance)
spot: Can you see a dancer's twists and turns in the shapes?
story: Picabia was inspired by a dancer he watched on a ship to New York. He painted the energy of the dance, not the dancer.

title: The Cyclist
spot: Count the cyclist's legs and wheels. Why does it look like so many?
story: Goncharova painted the bike over and over, like frames of a film, to show speed. Look for words on the signs behind him.

title: Red and Blue Rayonism (Beach)
spot: Follow the streaks of light. Which way do they shoot?
story: Larionov invented Rayonism: painting the rays of light bouncing off things instead of the things themselves.

title: Glass
spot: Can you find glasses and bottles hidden in the rays?
story: Larionov painted how light shatters into streaks as it passes through glass. He and Natalia Goncharova were a couple.

title: Fate of the Animals
spot: Find a blue deer, a horse and some foxes in the chaos.
story: Part of this painting was burned in a fire. Marc's friend Paul Klee repainted the damaged corner. Can you tell which part?

title: Fighting Forms
spot: Find the red shape and the dark blue shape. Which one is winning?
story: One of Marc's last paintings. The animals are gone, leaving just two forces swirling into each other.

title: Four Trees
spot: Which of the four trees is different? Look at the stripes in the sky.
story: Schiele is famous for twisty portraits, but he loved painting trees too, giving each one its own personality.

title: Gelmeroda IV
spot: Find the church steeple. How many sharp points can you count?
story: Feininger painted this little village church in Germany more than a dozen times. He also drew comic strips for a Chicago newspaper.

title: Love (Abstract Head)
spot: Find the eyes, the nose and the mouth. Is this face awake or dreaming?
story: Jawlensky painted hundreds of simple faces like this one, using just a few lines and colours.

title: Chromatic Fantasy
spot: Is this a pattern, a garden or a stained-glass window?
story: Giacometti also designed stained-glass windows, and he painted colour so it seems to glow like glass.

title: Synchromy in Orange: To Form
spot: Find the spiral of colours. Can you see a figure hidden inside it?
story: Russell co-invented "Synchromism," which means "with colour." He believed colour could work like music.

title: Composition VI
spot: Which shapes look flat, and which look 3D?
story: Bruce studied in Paris with Henri Matisse. Later he destroyed many of his own paintings, so only a small number survive.

title: Battle of Lights, Coney Island
spot: Find the rides and the electric lights. Can you almost hear the noise?
story: Stella painted Coney Island's amusement park at night, when thousands of new electric lights made it glow.

title: Merz 50. Composition
spot: Find the number 50 and scraps of paper with printing on them.
story: Schwitters made art from things he picked up off the street: tickets, wrappers and labels. He called it "Merz."

title: Composition
spot: Find the circles and the squares. Which colour appears only once?
story: Taeuber-Arp was a dancer, puppet-maker and designer as well as a painter. Her face was on the Swiss 50-franc note.

title: Primordial Chaos, No. 16
spot: Find the spirals and the letters.
story: Some of the earliest abstract paintings ever made. Af Klint believed she was guided by spirits as she painted this series.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 3, Youth
spot: Find the flower shapes and the little spirals.
story: The Ten Largest show the stages of life, from childhood to old age. Each painting is over three metres tall.

title: Altarpiece No. 1
spot: Find the rainbow staircase and the golden sun.
story: Af Klint designed this series to hang in a spiral-shaped temple that was never built.

title: Shimmering Substance
spot: Look for yellow and white. Does it shimmer when you look away and back?
story: Painted just before Pollock's famous drip paintings, with thick paint pressed straight from the tube.

title: Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)
spot: Do the lines look like dancing, rain or branches?
story: Pollock laid huge canvases on the floor and dripped and flung paint from above, walking all around them. This one is over 5 metres wide.

title: Convergence
spot: Find red, yellow, blue and orange all tangled together.
story: Pollock used house paint and sticks instead of brushes. People still argue about whether "anyone could do that." Could you?

title: Slow Swirl at the Edge of the Sea
spot: Find the two figures. Do they look like people, birds or sea creatures?
story: Before his famous colour blocks, Rothko painted dreamy creatures. This may be a picture of him and his wife, Mell.

title: No. 61 (Rust and Blue)
spot: Stare at the blue band for 30 seconds. Do the edges start to glow?
story: Rothko wanted people to stand close to his big paintings so the colour would wrap around them.

title: Orange and Yellow
spot: Where does the orange end and the yellow begin?
story: Rothko painted many thin layers, so his colours seem to float and glow from inside.

title: Exotic Landscape
spot: Find the monkeys and the oranges. How many kinds of leaves are there?
story: Rousseau never saw a jungle. He painted these after visiting the botanical garden and zoo in Paris, and he taught himself to paint.

title: Sunset
spot: Find the sun and its reflection. How many colours are in the sky?
story: Vallotton was also famous for bold black-and-white woodcuts. Here he turned a sunset into simple bands of colour.

title: The Jack Pine
spot: Find the snowy hills far away. What time of day is it?
story: Thomson painted this from a sketch made in Algonquin Park. It's one of the best-known paintings in Canada.

title: The Tangled Garden
spot: Find the tall sunflowers bending over. Why are they drooping?
story: MacDonald painted his own garden in Thornhill, just north of Toronto. Critics in 1916 disliked it; now it's a Canadian classic.

title: The Solemn Land
spot: Find the river winding between the hills.
story: Painted in Algoma, northern Ontario, where the Group of Seven travelled and lived in a railway boxcar to sketch.

title: Autumn
spot: How many different leaf colours can you find?
story: Carmichael was the youngest member of the Group of Seven. He also taught at the Ontario College of Art in Toronto.

title: Lone Lake
spot: Find the lake. How many hills are stacked one behind another?
story: Carmichael loved the rolling hills of northern Ontario and smoothed them into simple, stacked shapes.

title: Mount Lefroy (sketch)
spot: Follow the ridges up to the peak. Where is the snow?
story: Mount Lefroy is in the Rockies near Lake Louise. Harris painted mountains as smooth, glowing shapes, almost like sculptures.

title: Scorned as Timber, Beloved of the Sky
spot: Find the one tall, skinny tree left standing.
story: Loggers left this tree because it was too thin to be worth cutting. Carr made it the hero, reaching for the sky.

title: Ejiri in Suruga Province
spot: Find the papers flying in the wind and the hat blowing away. Where is Mount Fuji?
story: This is from the same series as Hokusai's famous Great Wave. Here Fuji is just a simple white outline.

title: Fireworks at Ryōgoku
place: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
spot: Find the boats on the river. Where did the firework burst?
story: Summer fireworks over the Sumida River in Edo, now called Tokyo. The festival still happens every year.

title: Cats as the 53 Stations of the Tōkaidō
spot: How many cats can you count? Find one with a fish.
story: Kuniyoshi loved cats and kept many in his studio. Each cat's pose is a pun on the name of a stop along an old road.

title: Evening at Ushibori
spot: Find the boat with its sail up. What time of day is it?
story: Hasui travelled all over Japan sketching quiet scenes like this one.

title: The Sumida River in the Mist
spot: Find the boats in the mist. Which one is closest?
story: Yoshida travelled the world, including North America, and turned what he saw into woodblock prints.

title: Kōnoshima
spot: Find the sailing boat and the island behind it.
story: Unusually for Japan at the time, Yoshida oversaw the carving and printing of his woodblocks himself.

title: Five Egrets Descending in Snow
spot: Count the egrets. Which one is about to land?
story: Koson made many bird prints for collectors in Europe and America. Egrets were one of his favourites.

title: Siphonophorae
spot: Is this one animal or many? Find the bell shapes at the top.
story: A siphonophore looks like one creature but is really a colony of tiny animals working together. Some are longer than a blue whale.

title: Ophiodea (brittle stars)
spot: Count the arms on each brittle star.
story: Brittle stars are cousins of starfish. If one loses an arm, it can grow it back.

title: Snowflakes (photographs)
spot: Find two snowflakes that look almost alike. How many points does each one have?
story: Bentley, a farmer in Vermont, was the first person to photograph a single snowflake, in 1885. He took more than 5,000 snowflake photos.

title: Scarlet Macaw
place: Illustrations of the Family of Parrots
spot: Find the macaw's feet and its curved beak.
story: Lear painted parrots when he was still a teenager. Later he became famous for funny poems like "The Owl and the Pussy-cat."

title: Pineapple
place: Metamorphosis of the Insects of Surinam
spot: Find the butterflies and the little insects.
story: Merian painted pineapples in Suriname, where they grew. Most people in Europe had never seen one.

title: Carolina Parakeet
spot: Count the parakeets. Which one is upside down?
story: The Carolina parakeet was the only parrot native to eastern North America. It went extinct in 1918.

title: British Algae (cyanotype)
spot: Find the delicate branches of the seaweed.
story: Atkins made one of the first books ever illustrated with photographs, using sunlight and chemicals that turn blue.

title: Plant Forms (photograph)
place: Art Forms in Nature (Urformen der Kunst)
spot: These are plant buds up close. Do they look like buildings or sculptures?
story: Blossfeldt taught art and used a homemade camera to magnify plants, showing his students nature's shapes.
